title: Victims of Groupthink
text:
In April 1961, a force of Cuban exiles trained and backed by the CIA landed at the Bay of Pigs. Within days the invasion had failed completely. Yale psychologist Irving Janis was struck that President Kennedy's advisers, among the ablest people in government, had approved such a weak plan.

Janis studied the Bay of Pigs and other American foreign policy failures, including the lack of preparation for Pearl Harbor, the decision to cross into North Korea in 1950 and the escalation in Vietnam. He contrasted them with better handled decisions, such as the Cuban missile crisis and the Marshall Plan. His 1972 book named the pattern groupthink: a close-knit group, led by a respected figure and under pressure, comes to value agreement over a hard look at the options.

He described its signs: a sense of invulnerability, belief in the group's own morality, stereotypes of opponents, members censoring their own doubts, an illusion that everyone agrees, and self-appointed guardians who keep bad news away from the leader. Janis noted that Kennedy's team handled the missile crisis differently, with the president sometimes leaving the room so others would argue freely and with members assigned to challenge proposals.
lesson: A team that agrees too easily may be protecting its comfort. Invite outside critics, let the leader speak last and assign someone to test the plan.
source: Janis, I. L. (1972). Victims of Groupthink: A Psychological Study of Foreign-Policy Decisions and Fiascoes. Houghton Mifflin.
caveat: Later research has supported parts of the model but found that cohesion alone does not reliably produce groupthink, and historians debate some of the case readings.
place: Yale University Old Campus, New Haven, USA
